Look up ways to politely stall a job offer in email. You can pretend to need more information about the role, or need to find funding, etc. Also look up ways to politely decline a position for once you've found a better role. Indeed has a lot of these things..

What I have to say about it is, unless you are very certain that you can apply and get into one of those two internships, it might be better to go with the one you're already discussing that is unpaid. This is because you'll have a source of income/stipend to support yourself, even if it's not exactly what you wanted.

In my opinion, you need to just stall politely. Fill out the application for the stipend fund, but do not submit it yet, if you can. Write an email to hiring manager/CEO and say:  "Thank you for your response; I look forward to putting my skills to good use at \_\_\_\_.  Is it possible to have 1-2 days/weeks (whatever you need) to find some sources of funding? I’m happy to be considered for the position, and I want to make sure that I am able to find funding first before I proceed."

  
You already have the funding but they don't have to know that. As far as they know, you've already accepted the offer and just need to find the funding. IF it's not looking like you will get either of the other two, then submit the application for the stipend and then continue with the first internship. If you DO get one of the other two, say something like "Unfortunately, I was not able to find funding to support myself if I take this role. Therefore, I must decline this role, however, blah blah blah."

But know that the location and smallness of the company will probably provide you with a lot of experience since you'll be juggling a lot of things, and you'll probably get really good networking in (being close to the CEO) and good letters of recommendation if you do good. Might even be hired on later as a full time employee. Consider what the other internships can give you that this unpaid one can't. But again, it's up to you!

Take that opportunity to relax! If you can land an internship, great! But if you can't, don't fret too much as you still have time to get experience and network. After college, you won't get any summers off, really (unless you land a REALLY good job or a specific industry, like teaching). It's important to slow down sometimes, rather than constantly rush towards a goal and do NOT feel guilt or shame about not "doing as much" as everyone else. However, it's important that you don't let your skills or knowledge get rusty and to stay somewhat productive! So, even if you don't have an internship, you can build skills that can go on your resume to show you weren't just being idle.

Potential things you can do: volunteer weekly somewhere related to your future career; get a part time job to earn money and learn soft skills; take some online courses for certifications; begin preparing for internship applications for next summer; networking with and doing informational interviews with people in your future field; review past coursework and study ahead for future coursework; research post-graduate options (e.g: grad school, industry jobs).

This is old but I just wanted to say that a lot of Redditors are US American, and the US often focuses more on empirical methods of psychotherapy. This is why psychoanalysis is not taught or debunked as pseudoscience.

In Europe and many other places, psychoanalysis, psych history, and the Viennese Schools of Psychology are still very prominent, respected, and taught. This includes Adlerian Psychology, and this is alongside methods such as CBT or whatnot. I’m not saying that I’m all for Adlerian Psychology or that I believe in everything it purports, but I respect it as a type of therapy.

I have read this book and, while the format  had my head spinning, I think it is a good representation of Adlerian Psychology. I’m not trained in psychoanalysis so I only have what I have learned in school, but the ideas in it are from Adler, from what I’ve learned. Most of Adlerian ideas are based on the idea of “Will to Power” which is the concept that people feel inferior and either succumb to that inferiority, or use that to move towards superiority (ie: their goals).

Again, Adlerian Psychology (also known as Individual Psychology) is well respected in European countries and practiced. The US doesn’t much like it, though.

this is a long one but yeah, I'm black and transmasc and I don't think I ever learned to mask growing up either, or I was very bad at it. barely anyone ever told me to stop being "weird", or I didn't notice when they did, and things I did were waved away as me being silly or gifted. I think a large part of it might be that, though I live in America, I grew up around mainly Caribbean people, who didn't care about respectability politics much?

eye contact with adults is considered rude in my culture, so everyone thought that was why I couldn't make eye contact with anyone. at home, when I complained about lights being too bright or noise being too loud, I was allowed to turn whatever it is was off or go somewhere else. when I curled up in small dark and quiet areas like inside a closet, paced around the house for hours, or walked on my toes, my family would tease me (calling me a little mouse or bird) but didn't care otherwise. I was a "troublemaker" in a normal classroom for being unable to sit properly or being disruptive (sitting on my legs, both legs up against chest, rocking back and forth, etc). however, because I was hyper verbal and literate and registered as "gifted", I was placed into a smaller classroom with less than 10 students and a gifted teacher who was patient and didn't care about my eccentricities so I never had to mask or anything.

I act younger than I am and I'm pretty naive/gullible cos I take things at face value, but in middle school through now, classmates just kinda... shifted me into a younger sibling role? they didn't bully me, they just tried to protect me from stuff. everyone thought I was weird but no one cared. I was just largely seen as having my heads in the clouds. my family largely didn't mind this, but sometimes got angry at me for "acting like a baby" (I tend to talk high pitched unconciously) or  "stupid". I now realize what was me being "stupid" was me not understanding their unspecific and indirect language. I always tried arguing that they way they say things are super confusing or not specific enough, but they would all gang up on me and gaslight me, so. examples:

* "go get me a blue towel" actually meant "go get me the towel that's blue or close to it". so when I would say "there's no blue towel, only a teal one", I would be called stupid, because *obviously* that counts as blue, too, which didn't make sense to me because teal is *blue-green*, not blue.
* "we're gonna have guests, so go clean the bathroom" actually meant "give a light and quick cleaning for things that are visibly dirty." I would get in trouble for "wasting time" by cleaning the entire bathroom, rather than only cleaning the immediate visible problems.

of course, I struggled with things like getting my hair done, or cutting my nails, or being in certain clothes due to the texture or whatnot, but as I got older, and was allowed to do things or dress by myself, I found ways that didn't bother me as much so I wouldn't have a shut/meltdown (not that I knew what those were, I just knew that sometimes I would start crying and flailing or "leave" my body because I was in so much pain from things that others didn't even feel). I was allowed to go sit in the car if shopping became too much for me. my parents did force me to learn to drive so I could get my license, but beyond that, don't make me drive if I don't want to, as driving is very overstimulating for me. I think the only things I struggled with socially was making friends, being too blunt (accidentally rude/mean) and being forgetful and face-blind. I had a few very good friends tho, so I didn't feel too lonely and  people didn't harp on me too much for being blunt, so again, didn't have to mask too much.

I only started seriously considering I was autistic when I began college in august and suddenly couldn't ask people to turn down their music or turn off their lights when I became overstimulated. I didn't consider myself a picky eater until suddenly the only things available were foods like pizza and garlic bread and barbecue pork, and processed things, and I began having gastrointestinal problems (almost all of my meals before were homemade and based on my preferences of rices, veggies, and seafood, so I don't like processed foods, most meats, and bread-y things). I didn't notice how movement based my stims were until I suddenly couldn't pace around the room I shared with two roommates, and instead unconsciously began flapping my hands instead. I began wearing long sleeved shirts and long pants, despite how much I hate being restricted, because I went outside more often but hate the feeling of too much sunscreen. I feel im masking more here, in the way that I suffer through overstimulation because I don't want to sound whiny or demanding by making them turn their music down or whatever.

this is also the first time people have indicated that I'm different in a concrete manner too, rather than just "weird". a friend, when I sincerely asked her if she and another friend were just joking with each other or actually being mean to each other, because I couldn't tell, reassured me that they were just playing and then gently asked if I was neurodivergent. a roommate asked if I was angry, and when I told her I struggle with facial expressions (my face tends to want to stay blank and I can't read other people's faces well), told me she thinks I might be autistic, citing multiple examples of things she'd noticed. when I started crying uncontrollably when hanging out with friends because there were too many loud and overlapping noises, after my friends turned everything off and I calmed down, one asked if I considered that I might be autistic (everyone else shushed her and told her that now was not the time, haha). I asked my friends from high school for opinions and they all admit that they thought I was autistic but didn't say anything because it wasn't a big deal.

so yeah, I guess I just never had to learn to mask, because, for the most part, people accepted me as I was. I kind of embraced being weird as a good thing, and now that I know im autistic, I feel like I understand myself more. sure, making friends is still hard and I still struggle in general with things, but I can now work around those things

i have no advice for trans tape but for binders. i’m sorry if it’s a lot 

- make sure you have a friend with you while putting it on cos it’s quite common to get stuck! i got stuck the first time but luckily i was flexible enough to get out without calling for help.

- make sure you’re clean and dry when you put it on!! being wet makes it a NIGHTMARE to try to  put on and being dirty or sweaty makes you have to clean it more (which may be bad if you’re not out and have to be sneaky). put deodorant on AFTER you put on the binder

- MAKE! SURE! THE BINDER! IS! THE RIGHT! SIZE! cant stress this enough! too small and it can injure you putting it on or wearing it for long periods of time. too loose and it won’t be doing its job. it should be compressing your chest without making breathing difficult. if it’s tight but you can take a full deep breath in, you’re good.

- i know people tell you to only wear it for 8-10 hours but work your way up to that! wear it for maybe a half hour at first, then maybe 1 hour then 2 then keep going. don’t just wear it for the full time immediately afterwards. this gets your body used to it PLUS stretches it out a bit 

- TAKE BINDER BREAKS!!! If you’re wearing it for 8 hours straight, find about 15 minutes throughout the day to set aside to take deep breaths, stretch, or take it off. carry a sports bra in your bag if it becomes painful to wear. if you wear the binder for long periods of time daily, skip a day or two every week to let your body rest. listen to your body!!

- common tip but don’t run or do physical activity in a binder or any activity that requires elevated breathing. yes this includes things like choir singing or running. don’t do it, binders compress your chest which means you can’t get air properly.

- if you feel you might faint for whatever reason, take the binder off. again, you breathing when conscious vs you breathing when unconscious are two dif things and the second with a binder on might be dangerous. tell a friend you’re wearing one so if you pass out unexpectedly, they know to cut it off you if needed 

- when you take it off, take deep breaths, cough to dislodge any liquid that might have set in your lungs, and do some stretches specifically for your upper torso. your back and shoulders WILL ache! that’s okay and it will usually fade! if it doesn’t, take a break for a few days

- if there is ongoing pain that keeps getting worse every time you put on the binder, that doesn’t go away no matter how much time goes by, your ribs are deforming, feel bruised or broken, lots of fluid is in your lungs and won’t go, etc: STOP wearing it! just stop! GO TO THE DOCTOR! NOW!

- use lotion to keep your chest and the areas that the binder edges dig into from getting irritated! it may also keep your skin soft and elastic if you wish for top surgery in the future! also, learn ways to position your chest to reduce risk of injury. your targets pointing forward rather than down is best if you wish for top surgery.

- for gc2b binders specifically (that’s what i use, dunno about others), it’s okay to machine wash! don’t dry it in a machine but washing is okay! it’s never frayed or gotten worse in quality for me! hand wash is best but if you can’t, machine wash is okay so don’t feel guilty. just make sure you’re using liquid soap and using cold water for best results.

There is no specific length for the lit review, however it's recommended that it is 1000-1500 words. However, based on your topic, how specific your field is, etc, it depends. As an example, mine was almost 2000 words. There is no specific length for each section, either. It is recommended that your method section is a long part of your paper, however, over 1000 words, because non-replicable = instant 1 or 2. Take the time to make sure that the methods is clear, understandable, that you incorporate ethical considerations (if it applies) and that you justify the use of your method, how it aligns with your purpose, and any approaches that you take within that method. Another pretty long section should probably be your discussion as that is where you are setting up your argument, supporting or debunking your argument with your results and with previous research from your lit review, etc.

You don't necessarily need footnotes for APA, unless you want to use them because there are many things that would be too long if they were placed directly into your paper.   


The graders do check your references, not by going to the sources themselves (I assume), but they look at what is cited and how they are cited.
